papers.title: Brain pericytes are an oxidative stress-sensitive cell population damaged through ROS-1 dependent TRPA1 activation.
papers.abstract: Oxidative stress is a pathological process driven by an imbalance between the production and clearance of reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is a hallmark of numerous brain disorders, driving neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and neurodegeneration. Here, we used two-photon microscopy in rodent brain slices to evaluate cell-type vulnerability to oxidative stress. We identified a microvascular cell population displaying pronounced sensitivity to H2O2 and thiol oxidation. These Pdgfr-{beta} expressing cells were identified as pericytes and perivascular fibroblasts. Because pericytes regulate capillary perfusion and BBB integrity, we examined mechanisms driving their injury. Pericyte damage was independent of apoptosis or necroptosis, but required Ca2+ influx. While blocking voltage-gated Ca2+, TRPC, Orai channels was ineffective, inhibitors of TRPA1 channels reduced pericyte damage. Immunostaining and western blotting showed TRPA1 associated with brain capillaries and pericytes. Functionally, TRPA1 regulated uptake of the pericyte-selective marker NeuroTrace, whereas pericyte GCaMP6f imaging demonstrated that TRPA1 was not the primary driver of cytosolic Ca2+ elevations during oxidative stress. These findings establish pericytes as vulnerable targets of oxidative stress and implicate TRPA1 as a mediator of pericyte structural degeneration. This sensitivity to oxidative stress, mediated by ROS-TRPA1 coupling, could contribute to the pericyte stress and degeneration observed in brain pathology.

papers.title: Alzheimer's Disease-Associated Proteomic Changes in Olfactory Stem Cells Show Pathway-Level Transcriptomic Overlap
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive, neurodegenerative disorder and the leading cause of dementia worldwide. Although recent therapeutic advances have provided some disease-modifying potential, there is currently no curative treatment for AD, highlighting the need for improved disease models and early biomarkers. Olfactory mucosal stem cells, which can be expanded in vitro as olfactory neurosphere-derived (ONS) cells, represent a promising source for biomarker discovery because olfactory tissue is more accessible than central nervous system tissue and has been reported to exhibit AD-related pathological changes. In this study, we used subcellular fractionation-based proteomics, reconstructed bulk proteomics and integrated transcriptomic-proteomic analyses to characterise alterations in ONS cells derived from healthy control, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD individuals. Fraction-specific proteomics identified cytoplasmic and nuclear-enriched protein abundance changes, including alterations in proteins and pathways associated with cytoskeletal organisation, RNA processing, intracellular trafficking, autophagy and mitochondrial/metabolic processes. Reduced LC3B abundance in cytoplasmic AD ONS cells was supported by western blot analysis, although LC3B abundance alone does not indicate altered autophagic flux. Reconstructed bulk proteomics identified 40 FDR-significant proteins in AD compared with HC, defining an AD-associated protein signature enriched for extracellular matrix, cytoskeletal, organelle-associated and RNA-processing pathways. Despite proteomic enrichment of mitochondrial and metabolic pathways, Seahorse Mito Stress Test analysis did not identify significant group-level differences in mitochondrial respiration. Integrated transcriptomic-proteomic analysis revealed partial RNA-protein concordance and pathway-level overlap across disease-associated processes. Together, these findings support the use of patient-derived ONS cells as a model for investigating AD- and MCI-associated molecular changes and highlight protein signatures for further validation.

papers.title: Modelling prodromal Parkinson's disease- gastrointestinal pathology and early motor deficits in mice after transient rotenone exposure
papers.abstract: Early gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is a hallmark feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet models capturing prodromal gut and brain pathology in PD remain limited. Motivated by the increased PD risk associated with pesticide exposure, we monitored motor behavior, brain pathology, and GI structure and function over 9 months following 5 daily doses of rotenone in mice. Transient rotenone exposure induced significant nigrostriatal pathology, including {approx}48% loss of dopaminergic neurons and increased -synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra, without significant changes in gross motor function. Notably, we identified pronounced GI dysfunction including reduced colonic transit velocity, altered motility dynamics, and delayed whole-gut transit. These functional changes were accompanied by enteric dopaminergic neurodegeneration, increased colonic -synuclein accumulation, increased colonic crypt depth, goblet cell hyperplasia with elevated mucin content per goblet cell. The findings are consistent with prodromal PD, suggesting the utility of this model for investigating early disease mechanisms and intervention strategies.

papers.title: Sound-Driven Motion of Human Cochlear Structures Depends on Organ of Corti Integrity
papers.abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) was used to image and measure the passive sound-driven displacements of cochlear structures in situ through the intact round window membrane of fresh human cadaveric specimens at 12 to 30 hours postmortem. We find that the anatomical integrity of the organ of Corti (OoC) affects cochlear structural motion. OoC with high integrity (erect with supporting cells) have small osseous spiral lamina (OSL) motion. Conversely, OoC with low integrity (flattened without supporting cells) have large OSL motion. For the ratio of motion between the basilar membrane (BM) and OSL (BM/OSL), OoC with high integrity has large BM/OSL motion while a cochlear partition without OoC has small BM/OSL motion. Furthermore, the high-integrity OoC has reticular lamina surface motion that is lower than the BM, whereas low-integrity OoC has similar reticular lamina and BM motion. This relationship between OoC anatomical integrity and cochlear structural motion will have consequential effects on sound transduction.

papers.title: A genome-wide catalog of sites where peripheral DNA methylation reflects the brain
papers.abstract: Epigenetic studies of psychiatric and neurological disorders rely largely on peripheral tissues, yet where peripheral DNA methylation (DNAm) reflects the brain remains unclear. We generated a paired brain and peripheral DNAm dataset from 148 donors in three cohorts and combined it with five published cohorts for consensus brain-peripheral correlations. By cross-validation across cohorts, we defined brain epigenome shared sites (BrESS), more than 100,000 CpGs per tissue at which peripheral DNAm reproducibly predicts brain DNAm. BrESS lay at promoters active in both brain and periphery and in housekeeping genes, and most were not explained by genetic effects. BrESS did not contribute to the heritability of seven disorders, and CpGs from epigenome-wide association studies of these disorders were not enriched at BrESS. Peripheral DNAm reflects the brain mainly in a regulatory compartment shared across tissues, outside which disease signals largely lie, and BrESS separate peripheral signals attributable to the brain from others.

papers.title: Engineered proteins to restore and enhance neurotransmitter release
papers.abstract: Synapse dysfunction is a hallmark feature of many neurological diseases. Synaptic transmission is initiated in nerve terminals, where active zone protein complexes control vesicle fusion for neurotransmitter release. Here, we engineer proteins that mediate active zone functions and demonstrate their use for reconstituting and strengthening neurotransmission. A protein composed of CaV{beta}4 and the RIM1 zinc finger, {beta}4-Zn, restored neurotransmitter release after active zone disruption through recruitment of Munc13. We develop {beta}4-MC, derived from the Munc13-1 MUN and C2C domains, which bypasses Munc13 recruitment and directly mediates vesicle docking, priming and fusion after active zone disruption. In {beta}4-MC, MUN domain functions are dispensable for docking, but active MUN and C2C domains are both necessary for neurotransmitter release. In wild-type mouse and human neurons, {beta}4-MC but not {beta}4-Zn strengthens neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, {beta}4-Zn and {beta}4-MC restore and enhance dopamine release in the mouse striatum, respectively. Hence, {beta}4 proteins are engineered secretory proteins with therapeutic potential as enhancers of synaptic function.

papers.title: Muscarinic signaling sustains delay-period selectivity in prefrontal cortex by preserving thalamic drive
papers.abstract: Short-term memory (STM) requires the temporary maintenance of task-relevant information in prefrontal cortex (PFC). Reciprocal interactions between the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and PFC have been implicated in sustaining this activity, but how thalamofrontal communication is maintained despite the biophysical constraints of repetitive synaptic transmission remains unclear. Here, we show that MD--PFC synapses exhibit profound frequency-dependent short-term depression, causing repetitive thalamic input to progressively lose its ability to drive PFC neurons. During STM performance, acetylcholine (ACh) levels in PFC rose rapidly following cue presentation and remained elevated throughout the delay period. Muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) activation did not alleviate synaptic depression, but instead increased the intrinsic excitability of PFC neurons, thereby preserving their responsiveness to weakened thalamic input. Conversely, mAChR blockade impaired STM performance and progressively disrupted delay-period directional representations at both the single-neuron and population levels, while largely sparing initial encoding. These findings identify muscarinic signaling as a postsynaptic gain mechanism that compensates for declining thalamofrontal efficacy and sustains task-relevant prefrontal representations during STM.

papers.title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
papers.abstract: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.

papers.title: Nanoscale remodeling of synaptic glutamate receptors and calcium channels in temporal lobe epilepsy
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of focal epilepsy and remains drug-resistant in approximately one-third of patients, for whom surgical resection of the epileptogenic zone is currently the most effective treatment option. One strategy to improve therapeutic outcomes involves identifying the molecular mechanisms and key regulators underlying synaptic function. Although altered glutamatergic neurotransmission is considered a major contributor to epileptic hyperexcitability, the nanoscale organization of key synaptic proteins in the human epileptic cortex is still not well characterized. In particular, it remains unclear whether pre- and postsynaptic proteins undergo synapse-type-specific remodeling in TLE. Here, we used high-resolution freeze-fracture replica immunolabeling to map the nanoscale organization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (AMPARs) and presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2.1) in glutamatergic synapses of cortical layers II/III of surgically resected human tissue. We examined perilesional, cytologically unremarkable, non-epileptogenic cortical tissue obtained from patients undergoing tumor resection (52-63 years; two female and three male patients) and compared these data with cortical samples from patients with refractory TLE (22-53 years; two female and four male patients). To assess whether pathological remodeling differs across synapse populations, we analyzed both excitatory dendritic spine and shaft synapses. We found a robust, highly consistent increase in AMPAR density at both spine and shaft synapses in TLE patients indicating enhanced postsynaptic excitatory signaling. However, AMPAR spatial reorganization differed between synapse types. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that spine synapses largely preserved a random receptor distribution without a significant clustering pattern, whereas shaft synapses exhibited a redistribution from clustering toward random receptor arrangements together with reduced center-preference within the postsynaptic density. In contrast, presynaptic CaV2.1 remodeling was more variable and predominantly associated with excitatory spine synapses. TLE spine synapses exhibited an overall increase in CaV2.1 density together with significantly larger and more numerous CaV2.1 nanoclusters within the active zone. This difference was particularly pronounced in male patients. In comparison, shaft synapses displayed only minor presynaptic alterations. CaV2.1 channels remained highly clustered under both control and epileptic conditions, indicating preservation of core active-zone organizational features despite disease-associated nanoscale remodeling. Together, these findings provide direct ultrastructural support that pathological plasticity in human TLE involves an overall increase in excitatory postsynaptic responsiveness and a target cell-specific increase of excitatory release probability at cortical synapses.

papers.title: Classic and novel features of the dentate gyrus vascular niche quantified through 3D vessel reconstruction
papers.abstract: Adult neurogenesis, the continued generation of new neurons throughout life, supports a variety of emotional and cognitive functions in mammals. Lifelong neurogenesis occurs in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, where a neurogenic niche supports the survival and growth of neural stem cells (NSCs), which divide to generate new neurons. A key component of this niche is the surrounding vasculature, thought to give NSCs access to circulating support molecules, oxygen, and nutrient metabolites. The DG vasculature is strikingly variable across layers. Vascular density and linearity, for example, have been noted to differ substantially in the different cell layers that make up the DG. Most of these prior descriptions of the DG vasculature have been qualitative, and other important aspects of vessel morphology, like vessel diameter, have not been previously reported to our knowledge. To provide a more complete and quantitative description of the adult DG vasculature, we used a 3D imaging technique to fully characterize the vasculature of each DG cellular layer. Our 3D reconstructions of DG blood vessels provide a quantitative method for measuring several known, qualitative features of the neurogenic niche, such as blood vessel density and tortuosity. In some cases, we reproduce qualitative observations, such as affirming that vessel density is high in the subgranular zone (SGZ) where NSCs reside and low in the granule cell layer. In other cases, our findings go counter to what qualitative observations suggest. For example, the SGZ is often described as having uniquely linear blood vessels, but we found that linearity was similar between the SGZ and hilus layer. We also report new measures of features of DG layer vascular architecture: vessel diameter and branching. Together, these findings offer a global, quantitative characterization of the DG vascular niche in adult mice. Beyond providing more detailed characterization of DG vasculature, we also anticipate our methods and estimates of variance in mice will be useful for investigators wishing to plan their own quantitative studies of changes in the vascular structure of the DG.

papers.title: Alpha-synuclein and neuromelanin converge to promote Parkinsons disease pathology
papers.abstract: Parkinsons disease (PD) is defined by the preferential degeneration of neuromelanin (NM)-containing dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra (SN), accompanied by intraneuronal inclusions rich in alpha-synuclein (aSYN). However, the mechanistic relationship between NM accumulation and aSYN pathology remains unclear. Here, we reveal a bidirectional pathogenic relationship between aSYN and NM. In human post-mortem midbrain tissue, ventral nigral neurons with high NM content display increased aSYN mRNA expression and are preferentially lost in PD. In a rat model that recapitulates age-dependent, human-like NM accumulation via targeted tyrosinase (TYR) expression, co-expression of aSYN accelerates NM buildup, enhances aSYN oligomerization, and aggravates nigrostriatal degeneration. Mechanistically, aSYN oligomerization in NM-producing rats decreases vesicular dopamine storage and impairs vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane, increasing cytosolic dopamine availability for oxidation into NM. Together, these findings support a pathogenic feedback loop in which elevated aSYN accelerates NM synthesis through disrupted dopamine compartmentalization, while NM accumulation further promotes aSYN aggregation and neuronal loss. This aSYN-NM axis may underlie the preferential vulnerability of pigmented nigral neurons in PD and provide a mechanistic framework for the development of future targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: Open-source virtual reality platform for head-fixed adult zebrafish
papers.abstract: Virtual realities (VRs) are powerful tools to study how brains interact with the world through behavior. We present a new platform for closed-loop high-resolution virtual-reality experiments in head-fixed adult zebrafish. The VR is defined using open-source software, projected onto a semi-hexagonal tank by three projectors, and controlled by software allowing for modular trial-and-block experimental designs. Real time VR updates are performed by an optimized algorithm based on infrared tail videos. Two-photon imaging during behavior is achieved by custom gating of VR projectors and coordinated with stimulus triggers by a microcontroller. Using this system we found that fish respond to visual landmarks in virtual corridors with distinct changes in locomotion parameters and body posture. Adding landmarks to a familiar corridor elicited localized behavioral responses that decayed with experience. Restricting the viewing distance by simulating 'murky water' further confirmed that behavioral responses were driven by the visibility of landmarks independent of their position. Our platform provides a user-friendly, versatile VR system for the joint analysis of neuronal activity and behavior in adult zebrafish

papers.title: Predicting alcohol consumption from resting-state functional connectivity: Feature relevance and the potential of meta-matching.
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is among the most prevalent mental disorders. Associations between resting-state fMRI functional connectivity (FC) and AUD have been reported but rarely replicated. In this preregistered study, we investigated the extent to which FC predicts alcohol consumption, as measured by the AUDIT-C score, in a large sample of non-treatment-seeking alcohol consumers (N = 739), including 528 participants with varying degrees of AUD severity. To optimize performance, we compared kernel ridge regression (KRR) trained directly on this sample with transfer-learning models based on multilayer meta-matching embeddings, from which we derived data-driven relevance maps at the connection, region, and network levels. We tested split-half reliability, reproducibility across cohorts, and outcome specificity of the relevance maps. Both models predicted AUDIT-C scores moderately but significantly (r {approx} 0.15). Meta-matching did not outperform KRR in prediction. Relevance maps showed limited split-half reliability, consistent with the modest predictive performance, but reproduced moderately well across two independent cohorts. These maps indicate reduced connectivity among limbic regions, the anterior middle temporal gyrus, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal attention network regions. In contrast, hypothesized hyperconnectivity patterns involving the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus were less reliable and mostly non-significant. Overall, our findings suggest that resting-state FC contains reproducible but weak signals related to alcohol consumption. Transfer learning improved relevance-map reliability but not prediction performance and reduced outcome specificity. These results support the utility of interpretable machine learning for identifying connectivity patterns related to drinking behavior, while also highlighting current limitations in its predictive power.

papers.title: Disentangling evoked and induced activity from single-trial neurophysiological time series
papers.abstract: Evoked and induced responses are fundamental neurophysiological readouts in the development and assessment of treatments for disorders with impaired neural function. Distinguishing these responses is essential for interpreting single-trial variability, identifying the determinants of these responses, and enabling real-time probing of cortical responsiveness. However, because of dynamic overlap, separating evoked and induced activity remains unsolved at the single-trial level when instantaneous fluctuations of cortical responsiveness are of interest. We developed the Evoked-Ongoing/Induced Separator (EOIS), a framework for separating event-evoked, ongoing, and event-modulated induced activity from single-trial data. EOIS recovers evoked and ongoing/induced components by leveraging their distinct phase-consistency features in MEG and real-time EEG, enabling subject-agnostic single-trial time-series analysis and attribution of cortical response variability to specific components. By delivering component-resolved time series, EOIS enables biomarker refinement, pharmacodynamic readouts, and closed-loop neuromodulation, facilitating translational deployment across individuals and care settings.

papers.title: Artificial hibernation uncovers distinct interaction dynamics in functional and pathological state change
papers.abstract: Neural population activity can reorganize without disrupting function, but how such changes differ from those associated with pathology remains unknown. Artificial hibernation, Q-neuron-induced hypothermia and hypometabolism (QIH), causes extensive synaptic remodeling in the hippocampus without erasing established memories, allowing us to examine how extensive network reorganization can occur without lasting functional impairment. Longitudinal calcium imaging showed that hippocampal activity recovered after QIH without returning to its pre-hibernation population configuration. Instead, QIH reorganized neuronal activity patterns and coactivity beyond representational drift. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that this reorganization of neuronal interactions depended on the preceding network state. In mice subjected to kainic acid-induced status epilepticus, QIH reduced seizure-associated increases in neuronal interactions and spike coactivity during sharp-wave ripples. Over the following 50 days, the divergence of hippocampal LFP trajectories was constrained, and the progressive development of electrophysiological and histological pathology was attenuated. These findings suggest that controlled, extensive reorganization of neural population activity can prevent the progression toward pathological network states, with changes in neuronal interactions, particularly sharp-wave ripple-associated coactivity, accompanying this process.

papers.title: Partial lesions of hypocretin neurons of the rat lateral hypothalamus affect wake and sleep regulation under increased sleep pressure
papers.abstract: Hypocretin(orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area are important for sleep and wake regulation in mammals and their damage in humans manifests clinically as narcolepsy. While in previous studies experimentally induced massive loss of these neurons revealed their physiological importance, small lesions and their manifestations can uncover more subtle features of sleep regulation and help understand the delicate processes in early stages of pathogenesis of narcolepsy. We studied the effects of partial lesions (approximately 30%) of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus on sleep patterns and EEG in rats. The lesions did not change the normal sleep and wake pattern in undisturbed rats. The effects of lesions manifested under increased sleep pressure after six hours of sleep deprivation, when they led to accelerated dynamics of compensatory slow wave sleep. The lesions also led to a slight decrease in theta frequency in wakefulness and in REM sleep, which we observed during undisturbed sleep and wake behavior as well as after sleep deprivation.

papers.title: Early development of cerebellar functional connectivity
papers.abstract: The cerebellum makes a critical contribution to cognitive and behavioural function, extending well beyond motor control, and is recognised as an important determinant of neurodevelopmental outcome. Despite this, little is known about the foundations of cerebellar functional organisation in early life. Addressing this gap is essential for establishing typical developmental trajectories against which atypical development can be assessed. Here, we analysed fMRI data from term-born neonates (n=155) scanned between 37 and 44 weeks postmenstrual age and mapped intra-cerebellar and cerebro-cerebellar functional connectivity across multiple levels of organisation. We identified 13 intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) within the neonatal cerebellum that recapitulated adult subdivisions, with two ICNs showing age-related increases in coverage and strength. Analysis of cerebro-cerebellar connectivity identified 15 sensory, motor and association cerebral clusters, seven increasing connectivity with age. Functional gradient analysis identified a continuous axis from somatomotor to association regions within intra-cerebellar and cerebro-cerebellar organisation, which became more pronounced with age. Together, these findings suggest that the foundations of adult cerebellar functional organisation are present at birth but undergo rapid and regionally heterogeneous maturation over the first weeks of postnatal life. This developmental framework provides a normative reference for understanding cerebellar development and its implications for later neurodevelopmental variation.

papers.title: The multi-scale geometry of neural encoding
papers.abstract: As recorded neural populations become larger and artificial networks more powerful, there is growing interest in understanding and comparing what different populations encode. Representational geometry offers a powerful way to characterise this: it remaps stimulus space to stretch well-encoded stimulus differences while shrinking poorly encoded ones. However, this remapping can be constructed in many ways from neural responses. Here, we introduce a multi-scale representational geometry, derived from first principles, that captures how neurons encode stimulus differences at every scale. It is exactly related to mutual information, so independent of decoding assumptions. The more a stimulus difference contributes to information, the more the geometry stretches it. Applied to spatial, motor and visual codes, it shows how neurons combine to encode information, how areas differ, and which features are best encoded. A single framework thus maps the structure of encoded information, uniting geometric and information-theoretic views of neural coding.

papers.title: Predictive dendrites as a foundation for biological learning
papers.abstract: A fundamental challenge for neuroscience is to identify laws of synaptic plasticity that are consistent with experimental observations at the level of individual neurons, whilst also explaining the ability of neural networks to learn complex tasks. Here we investigate a candidate law in which neurons adjust synaptic strengths to minimize the mismatch between somatic and dendritic activity. We demonstrate that models based on this rule can effectively adjust synaptic weights across network layers to learn non-linear tasks. Moreover, minimizing mismatch between spiking activity and dendritic inputs leads to integrate-and-fire dynamics and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The model reproduces the experimentally observed dependencies of plasticity upon initial synaptic weights and spike patterns, whilst also generating a series of testable predictions. Our results show that a single principle - minimization of somato-dendritic mismatch - links learning at the network level with fundamental properties of individual neurons, including membrane potential dynamics and canonical features of synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: Unstable word form representations and greater reliance on right hemisphere during word learning in adults with a history of developmental language disorder
papers.abstract: Impairment in acquiring new vocabulary is a persistent deficit in developmental language disorder (DLD), but its cortical substrates remain unclear. We investigated learning of new words in young adults with DLD and typically developing (TD) control participants using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Participants were exposed to spoken real words and two sets of pseudowords, with shared beginnings, in two MEG sessions. One set of pseudowords was actively trained for three days, paired with fantasy animal pictures. Both groups learned new pseudowords, but adults with DLD recalled fewer items and confused similar sounding pseudowords more often than TD adults. MEG recordings revealed robust left temporal learning effects in both groups, along with left inferior frontal involvement. The DLD group additionally showed stronger right-hemispheric involvement and a significant right temporal learning effect for the newly learned words. Furthermore, only the DLD group showed changes in the left and right temporal responses for the real words after the learning phase, indicating altered lexical access for familiar words after integration of new word forms with overlapping phonology into the mental lexicon. Together, the findings suggest persisting problems in creating and accessing stable and distinctive phonological memory representations for word forms in adults with DLD, along with altered hemispheric balance in processing.

papers.title: Pediatric brain charts reveal ADHD biotypes with distinct developmental, molecular, and therapeutic profiles
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large - scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross - ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra - normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra - normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain-behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra-normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra-normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra-normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype-specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome-wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

papers.title: Human and Mouse Models of the Bipolar Disorder-Associated ANK3 p.W1989R Variant Display Altered Somatostatin Interneuron Connectivity and Function
papers.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a debilitating neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent mood perturbations, cognitive and functional impairment, and increased risk of suicide. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have repeatedly identified the gene ANK3, which encodes the neuronal scaffolding protein ankyrin-G, as a risk locus for BD. Ankyrin-G interacts directly with the GABAA receptor-associated protein (GABARAP) to stabilize inhibitory synapses, providing a potential mechanistic link between ANK3 variation and GABAergic dysfunction observed in BD. Previously, we identified an ANK3 p.W1989R variant in a family with BD and demonstrated that this variant abolishes the ankyrin-G/GABARAP interaction, resulting in inhibitory signaling deficits in mice. Here, we investigated the effects of this variant in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons generated from an affected individual heterozygous for the ANK3 p.W1989R variant. CRISPR correction of the variant increased inhibitory synapse density on both glutamatergic and GABAergic patient-derived neurons. Integrated spatial transcriptomics and calcium imaging identified cell-type-dependent changes in gene expression and calcium dynamics. ANK3 p.W1989R somatostatin (SST) positive interneurons displayed altered calcium dynamics and reduced SST expression. To determine whether the variant impacts SST interneuron-mediated inhibition of cortical circuits, we selectively stimulated prefrontal cortical SST interneurons in heterozygous Ank3 p.W1989R mice and recorded optically evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (oIPSCs) from cortical pyramidal neurons. SST interneuron-mediated oIPSC peak amplitude, charge transfer, and decay times were reduced in variant mice, without a significant change in the paired-pulse ratio. These findings, using complementary human and mouse models, identify novel roles for ankyrin-G in SST interneuron-mediated inhibitory signaling and demonstrate that altered inhibitory connectivity and SST interneuron function are associated with ANK3 p.W1989R. This work provides mechanistic insight into how disrupted ankyrin-G-dependent synaptic function may contribute to inhibitory signaling deficits relevant to BD.

papers.title: Endogenous retrovirus activation disrupts postsynaptic organization in human glutamatergic neurons
papers.abstract: Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) comprise a substantial fraction of the human genome, yet whether their expression can directly alter human neuronal function remains unknown. Because glutamatergic signaling is fundamental to brain function and frequently disrupted in brain disorders, we asked whether activation of the primate-specific ERV-W group, associated with neurological disease, perturbs human glutamatergic neurons. We used CRISPR activation of the LTR17-ERV-W consensus sequence to examine its effects on neuronal and synaptic function, inducing transcription from multiple proviral loci, including five with intact open reading frames. Functionally, ERV-W activation selectively altered the postsynaptic compartment, reducing PSD-95 and NMDA receptor abundance. These changes were accompanied by altered excitatory synaptic transmission and reduced intrinsic excitability, whereas activation of ERVW-1/Syncytin-1 alone did not reproduce the phenotype. Our findings identify ERV-W activation as a modulator of human neuronal function with potential relevance to ERV-associated brain disorders.

papers.title: A critical assessment of LGN segmentation quality based on volume, contour, and location
papers.abstract: Reliable segmentation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a small thalamic relay nucleus essential for visual processing, is necessary for characterizing its anatomy in healthy populations and structural alterations in neurological disorders. However, accurate delineation remains challenging on routinely acquired T1-weighted images because the LGN is small, deeply located, and has limited contrast relative to surrounding thalamic tissue. Although manual segmentation remains the reference standard, it is time consuming and susceptible to rater variability, limiting its use in large datasets. Automated approaches may therefore provide a more scalable alternative. In this study, we performed a systematic benchmarking of seven automated approaches: FreeSurfer, NextBrain, DeepThalamus, HIPS-THOMAS, MASSP 2.0, BigBrain alignment, and manual novice segmentation against expert-defined ground truth. We applied a multi-metric evaluation incorporating the Dice similarity coefficient, Hausdorff distance and balanced average Hausdorff distance, volumetric similarity, and Euclidean distance. Together, these measures evaluate overlap, contour, volume, and location against expert manual segmentations. Our results indicate that HIPS-THOMAS and DeepThalamus outperformed the other automated methods in all metrics. However, manual segmentation retained high precision despite exhibiting greater inter-subject variance than the top-performing automated segmentation tools. The different metrics do not necessarily report the same order of quality, highlighting the need of using multiple metrics for evaluation segmentation quality.

papers.title: Differential value processing in the rostral and causal subthalamic nucleus during flexible and habitual decision-making in primates: Implications for cognitive dysfunction in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a major target region of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD), effectively alleviating motor symptoms. However, STN-DBS can also induce cognitive impairments, suggesting that the STN contributes to cognitive functions beyond simple motor control. Furthermore, anatomical organization supports functional segregation of cognitive processes, as basal ganglia subregions encoding flexible and stable values topographically project to distinct STN subregions. Yet, whether the STN contributes to cognitive functions and, if so, how subregions of the STN differentially process cognitive flexibility and habitual stability remains unknown. Here, we reveal a rostral-caudal functional organization of the STN that differentially supports flexible value updating and long-term value memory, enabling adaptive and habitual decision-making, respectively. Neurons in the rostral STN (rSTN) preferentially encode flexibly updated values, whereas neurons in the caudal STN (cSTN) preferentially encode stable long-term value memories. Notably, inactivation of the STN along the rostral-caudal axis produced dissociable behavioral deficits: rSTN inactivation selectively impaired goal-directed behavior requiring flexible value updating, whereas cSTN inactivation selectively disrupted habitual behavior guided by long-term value memories. Together, these results reveal a rostral-caudal functional segregation of the STN, with the rSTN supporting goal-directed behavior and the cSTN supporting habitual behavior. These findings further provide a framework for understanding how STN dysfunction or STN-DBS in Parkinson's disease may differentially affect cognitive processes beyond motor control.

papers.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

papers.title: A coordinated and reproducible multicellular response to AD pathology
papers.abstract: While single-cell measurements of the Alzheimer's disease (AD) brain allow investigation of vulnerable cells in unprecedented depth, reported findings are heterogeneous, mostly descriptive and often ignore interdependence of cellular responses. Operationalization of these findings requires a multi-cellular model of AD that is robust and reproducible. Here, we utilize a coordinated multicellular community approach across 2.3 million nuclei from 427 ROSMAP donors to identify robust multicellular axes associated with AD pathology and sex. The AD signature comprised profound alteration to RORB-GABRG excitatory neurons and disrupted oligodendrocyte precursor cell signaling. A separate set of AD-related cell-type specific molecular processes with strong sexual dimorphism also emerged. Importantly, these signatures developed and ROSMAP predicted neuropathology and sex, respectively, in a completely independent dataset (SEA-AD). These findings altogether summarize a highly consistent multi-cellular response to AD pathology in the human brain, creating a baseline cellular model to which perturbation and treatment experiments can be compared.

papers.title: Parvalbumin interneuron maturation reorganizes cortical population activity structure during development
papers.abstract: During brain development, spontaneous cortical activity undergoes a dramatic transformation from highly synchronous network events to less correlated and sparse neuronal firing that is thought to underlie more flexible neural coding. However, how the structure of population activity changes across this transition, what circuit mechanisms drive this reorganization, and the implications for information encoding have not been fully established. Using longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging in early postnatal mice, we demonstrate that cortical network desynchronization during the second postnatal week is accompanied by a redistribution of fractional variance from dominant, low-dimensional modes into many weaker dimensions, and a growing influence of GABAergic interneurons (INs) on the network. All-optical circuit interrogation revealed that parvalbumin (PV) INs, but not somatostatin (SST) INs, are sufficient to desynchronize the network and shift the distribution of population variance. Through targeted ablation of a fraction of PV INs, we show dimensionality is highly correlated with stimulus decoding accuracy. Furthermore, PV INs undergo a sharp increase in transcriptional maturation between postnatal day (P) 8 and 11, during which they preferentially enrich for synaptic genes. Lastly, a novel, biologically plausible, multi-cell-type computational model reproduced the developmental desynchronization and rise in dimensionality. Strikingly, without being constrained by perturbation data, the model accurately predicted the effects of each IN class on the network that we observed empirically.

papers.title: Splanchnic-spinal transmission of gut-initiated α-synucleinopathy
papers.abstract: Gut-initiated -synucleinopathy is proposed to spread from the gastrointestinal tract to the CNS, contributing to Parkinson's disease (PD), but whether routes beyond the vagus nerve are involved remains unclear. Using complementary intracolonic rotenone and gastroduodenal -synuclein PFF models, we combined pathway-specific surgical interruption with longitudinal behavioral analysis and anatomical mapping of pathological -synuclein. In the intracolonic rotenone model, interruption of the prevertebral ganglia/splanchnic-spinal axis more strongly attenuated behavioral deficits and -synuclein pathology than vagotomy. In the gastroduodenal PFF model, both vagal and splanchnic-spinal pathways contributed to pathology propagation. Early after PFF inoculation, pathological -synuclein was detected in peripheral neural structures associated with both routes. Consistent with these findings, spinal pathology was evident in human PD. Together, these results identify the splanchnic-spinal pathway as a key component of body-first Parkinson's disease, broadening current models of peripheral-to-central disease progression and informing efforts to target early peripheral disease progression.

papers.title: Slow Ionic Dynamics Reshape Bistability in a Biophysical Mean-Field Model of Brain Activity
papers.abstract: Brain states such as sleep, seizures, and resting wakefulness are often described in terms of transitions between distinct population states. Biophysically inspired mean-field models that couple neuronal firing statistics to slow ionic homeostasis provide a mechanistic bridge between detailed single-neuron physiology and macroscopic brain activity. Here we examine this issue in a biophysical mean-field model of cortical populations driven by potassium exchange and compare its dynamical repertoire with a matched spiking network across six physiological and pathological regimes. The fast subsystem contains a substantial region in which low- and high-activity fixed points coexist, but this conditional bistability is not inherited by the physiological resting branch of the complete slow-fast system. A generic fast-slow calculation identifies how feedback through a dynamical ionic variable changes the stability conditions of the fast subsystem, and an exact equilibrium reduction of the KIonEx-MF equations yields a single equilibrium on the physiological resting branch over the range examined. This resting state is excitable: perturbations generate intermittent synchronized events in both the mean-field and spiking-network descriptions. The results show how slow ionic dynamics can reshape conclusions drawn from a frozen fast subsystem and provide noise-driven excitability as an alternative route to spontaneous population transitions.
